utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. On this Monday, the 26th of February, 2007, I'd like to welcome all those in the courtroom. Mr. Scott and his lady colleagues, the Defence counsel, the accused who are sitting a long way away today because we're in a different courtroom. Today we have a witness who is going to take up the whole week. As far as the examination-in-chief is concerned, we gave six hours to the Prosecution, so the Prosecution will have six hours to examine the witness. And as far as the Defence teams are concerned, in view of the fact that this witness testimony will concern some teams more than others, Mr. Pusic will have one hour, 30 minutes; Mr. Coric will have one hour and 30 minutes as well; Mr. Stojic will also have an hour and 30 minutes; Mr. Prlic will have 45 minutes; and Mr. Praljak will have 45 minutes as well; and Mr. Petkovic will have 45 minutes too. Of course, it is up to you whether you wish to give your time to someone else or whether you're going to use that time up yourselves. In order to avoid any misunderstanding, Mr. Pusic will have one hour and 30 minutes. Mr. Coric will have one hour and 30 minutes, and Mr. Stojic will also have one hour and 30 minutes, because on the transcript it doesn't say hour, one hour. Now, I understood it that the Defence would like the floor before the witness is shown in, but before they say what they have to say and before I give the floor to Mr. Karnavas, I would like to say something. I was looking at the time used by both parties, and I have noted that with more than 500 hours of sitting that we had there was more than 100 hours of procedural issues discussed, which means more than 20 per cent of the overall Court time is taken up with procedural matters. Now, since we're trying to regulate procedural matters with written motions and with respect to requests for protective measures also in writing and evidence and exhibits in writing, notwithstanding all that we're still using up 100 of the 500 hours on procedural matters. I would prefer us to speak of fundamental matters rather than procedural matters. Of course, procedural matters always seem to be the same. So we would rather hear from the Defence and other parties about fundamental matters, because the procedural matters crop up again and again. Now, sometimes I am a little alarmed when I realise that we're wasting a lot of time raising objections, intervening, which, from my point of view, are of no interest. So the 100 hours that we have devoted to procedural matters could have been better used elsewhere dealing with fundamental issues, and this would have been more interesting all round, and probably for the Defence as well. Now I'm sure we're still going to discuss procedural matters. Who wants to take the floor? Mr. Karnavas, did you want to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I believe this is a fundamental matter as opposed to a procedural matter, and in fact we will only have to deal with it once even though it may apply to many witnesses that are to come. The witness that we are about to hear for the following four days was interviewed as a suspect. There are all sorts of documents that the Prosecution intends to introduce that bear the gentleman's signature. He was questioned extensively. In fact, if you do have his -- his statement, I have it right here, you can see it's about three or four inches thick, and we believe that it would be -- it's in the interest of justice and in the gentleman's interest if he was fully informed, one, that because he was viewed as a suspect at the time, and if you look at the content of the interview and the documents which bear his name that -- that he is exposed. The Prosecution in this case cannot immunise him. Yes, we have a completion strategy. Yes, the Security Council does not want this Tribunal to go on any further with any more cases, but you do have a Tribunal that is functioning in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the state court. In my previous case, witnesses that appeared for the Defence that were suspects are now defendants, accused, incarcerated as they are in the trial phase, and so we think that hence forward any of these so-called insiders, as they've been coined, who are suspects should be fully advised that their testimony here, and I think that it must be -- they must be told that the transcripts will be taken by this Prosecutor and given to the Prosecutor in Bosnia when so required. The other thing is - this is for future purposes - this particular gentleman was interviewed by Ms. Egels. Now, I notice that she won't be taking the witness, I take it, but in the future if we do come -- come up with a situation where a Prosecutor was involved in questioning the witness, that Prosecutor essentially also becomes a potential witness himself, and there would be a conflict of interest. So we think that this is something that may require the Court's consideration. But since that's not the case today, then we don't have to deal with this issue, but it's something you may want to give some thought to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. Karnavas. You spent three minutes, but since you're a professional and since I am also a professional, that question did not escape me, and here I have the article of the Rules of Procedure that I wanted to read. So I anticipated this problem, and rest assured that the matter quite certainly didn't escape me. Now, on to the next point with respect to Ms. Egels's participation and the interview with the "suspect." Now, we haven't deliberated this point, but it perhaps would be interesting to hear the view of Mr. Scott in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Mr. President, Judges. We couldn't disagree more with Mr. Karnavas's position. I guess that won't be the first or last time, but it is standard practice in this institution, has been for the last ten years, that suspect interviews are conducted. They often -- they often involve lawyers involved with the trial team. There are always -- there is always at least one investigator in the room. These are video recorded, which is a further assurance that everyone can have that the entire record is completely transparent for everyone to see. We do not see any conflict whatsoever, and in the future we do indeed anticipate, I don't know, but just so there's, again, transparency, but I certainly anticipate in the future a witness may indeed be taken by the lawyer in court who also interviewed that person previously. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber will give thought to the question raised by Mr. Karnavas, but I'm going to ask the usher to go and have the witness shown into the courtroom. While that is being done, the registrar, who is always mindful of the time, would like to give us two IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. So several parties have submitted some lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Mustafa Hadrovic, and the list submitted by OTP shall be given the Exhibit number IC 445, while the list submitted by 3D shall be given the Exhibit number IC 446. Finally, there has been a list -- actually, 5D has submitted a list of objections to documents tendered through -- tendered by the OTP through Witness DD. This list will be assigned Exhibit number IC 447.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Sir, would you stand, because you will be taking the solemn declaration. But first tell me whether you understand in your own language what I'm saying in your own language. So please tell me if you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, may have your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Josip Praljak, the 4th of November, 1952.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your occupation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am retired, a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you give me your date of birth again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 1952.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, do you have any family ties with General Praljak who is in the courtroom or do you just share the same surname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean you have the same name but you do not have any family ties with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do have. We do have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what are the family relationship -- what is the family relationship that you have with General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My late father and his late father were two brothers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you, sir, ever testified before an international or national court of law about the events that took place in your country or is this the first time that you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you now go ahead and read the solemn declaration handed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we go ahead I'd like to give you some information. You're going to be answering questions first put to you by the Prosecution, which I'm sure you have met, probably during the weekend. These questions will relate to your activity at Heliodrom, and for that the Prosecution has been given six hours. So during those six hours the Prosecution will be asking you questions. After that first stage the Defence teams and counsel sitting to your left will also be asking you questions, and the time for them has been distributed amongst the Defence counsel and the accused. Mr. Coric will have one hour, 30 minutes; Mr. Pusic will have one hour and 30 minutes; and Mr. Stojic will also have one hour and 30 minutes. The three other accused, who are Mr. Prlic, Mr. Petkovic, and General Praljak, will have 45 minutes each. However, they can decide to allocate each other any time necessary. Now, the four Judges sitting up at the bench in front of you can also ask you questions at any point in time, and I'm sure we shall be doing so, either to clarify certain answers that you have given to either of the two parties or because we have questions of our own and feel we need to ask those questions, because we have heard quite a lot of witnesses testifying about the Heliodrom. So our questions will follow on from what we have already heard. I would like to read out a Rule of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence which is very important and which you should be apprised of in view of your status as witness. It is Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Evidence and Procedure, and I'll read it out very slowly so that the interpreters can translate it for you, translate what I have said to you perfectly. This is what Rule 90(E) says: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." So this Rule applies to you and has three elements within it. The first element is to say that when you are asked a question, whether it be by the Prosecution, the Defence, or the Judges, if you consider it necessary you can say, "I do not want to answer that question because my answer would incriminate me." So taking that hypothesis, the Chamber can decide to hear the answer to the question nevertheless; however, if it does so, testimony compelled in this way cannot be used as evidence against you. It might seem complicated, but place your trust in the Judges and rest assured that they will apply the Rule to the letter. And this has never actually taken place in practice. It might be theory, but nonetheless it was necessary for me to apprise you of that Rule. Having said that, let me ask you to be as precise as possible in giving us your answers, because we are in oral proceedings here but supplemented by documents. So the Prosecution will be presenting you with documents in due course, and we have a number of binders full of documents which they intend to present to you. So your answers should be as precise as possible, because we need precision. We don't need approximations. Now, if at any point in time we feel that there has been some approximation, the Judges will ask you questions to be more specific and precise in your answers. If you don't understand a question, please do not hesitate to ask a person asking the question to rephrase it so that you can answer exactly what has been asked. You will also see that the way in which the questions are posed are very different depending on who is doing the asking. The Prosecution has one style and technique, the Defence has another, and the Judges have a third approach, so that you'll see that these approaches are not the same and the questions are asked in a different matter. But that is a technical point and need not concern you, because the essential point here is that you answer as exactly as possible the question that is being asked. If at any time during the proceedings you are feeling unwell, please do not hesitate to let us know, or if you're experiencing any difficulties, because four days of testimony in court is very tiring for a witness. I'm sure you'll leave the courtroom feeling extremely tired. So if you're feeling unwell or if you wish to take a break, please ask us. Generally we have a break every one and a half hours. We take a 20-minute break and then reconvene. But if at any point you're feeling incapable of continuing and not feeling well, we will make a break, because, as I say, it is very tiring, mentally and otherwise, to focus on the questions being asked and to provide your answers, and four days of testimony, five hours a day, means 20 hours during those two days of questions and answers, which is a very long time, and you might feel very tired. So as I've said, please tell us if you do. The Chamber is here to help you out if you experience any difficulties. Since you have already taken the solemn declaration, you are a witness in the pursuit of justice, which means that, as of now, you should not have any contact with the Prosecution. So this evening when you go back to your hotel, don't meet with anyone or talk to anyone from -- except the Witness and Victims Unit. So that in general terms is how the proceedings are going to be conducted this afternoon and this week, in fact. And we have devoted this whole week to your testimony. Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My colleague wants to make sure that you have perfectly understood the sense and the meaning of Rule 90(E) concerning self-incrimination. Have you understood it well, because if you haven't, then I can add to what I have already said. Can you answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understood well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you understood that if answering a question could possibly incriminate you, you can tell us, "I don't want to answer this question." You understood this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just saw the matter is clear to the witness. Of course Your Honour has properly advised him of the position under Rule 90(E). Your Honour, nonetheless, as I understand it, while that Rule would prevent any answers he might give from being used in a prosecution which might be brought before this Tribunal, I don't think it could confer that protection in -- in any proceedings that might be brought elsewhere. Your Honour, that may not be clear to the witness, and I wonder whether the Trial Chamber might think it appropriate to give that additional warning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Murphy. That did not elude me, of course. But we have another thing to add, Witness. When this Tribunal grants you protection, that protection concerns only your conduct before this Tribunal, not before any national court, so within this framework the Trial Chamber has another technical possibility. Let us imagine that you were asked a question and that answering it could incriminate you. Let's take a very simple example and you will understand. Let's imagine the warden of the prison or a deputy warden is outside his cell and sees a guard beating a prisoner and the warden and the deputy warden fail to do anything. You can say, "Yes, I was there. I saw it, but I did nothing," which means this Tribunal will not prosecute you for that. But in your own country, the prosecutor may use this against you, and in that case we, the Trial Chamber, have one possible course of action, and that is to move into private session or closed session so that nobody on the outside knows what you've said. Of course, this is purely hypothetical at this point, and we will play it by the ear and judge what is best in a particular situation. For the moment it is important that we make sure that you have perfectly understood the meaning of my warning. You confirmed it. Can you say again, "I understood it well"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I confirm I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, even if it's in closed session the Prosecution, if they were requested to provide a transcript of the gentleman's testimony to -- to Bosnia, to the state court, they would have to do so. Any -- because the gentleman is a suspect, you know, anything and everything that he says obviously can -- can be used against him. Any immunity that this Court grants to him, because that's in essence what you're doing, cannot be applied in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and even in closed-session testimony they will have to be -- that will need to be provided. That's -- that's my understanding at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you say, they will have, but the Trial Chamber may issue a decision stipulating that any such communication will only take place with the consent and approval of the Chamber. So I already have an answer to that. There is no question that you asked, in fact, Mr. Karnavas, so I can't answer it. We have already spent half of an hour on procedural matters, and I think we should finally start. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, Mr. President and Your Honours, ever so briefly. In talking to this witness, I don't have any reason to believe that any of these will actually -- any of these matters will actually present a problem. I understand this witness is here to speak completely candidly with the Chamber and provide his evidence. Just so the record is clear and there is no misunderstanding and there is no point in going into it now, but I reserve the position of the Prosecution. We may not in fact agree with some of the positions that have been stated by various Defence counsel asking that, so there's no point to belabour it at this juncture. I also extent my greetings to everyone else in the courtroom and to those helping us in the booths.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Praljak. I didn't get any translation. I don't know if anybody else did.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There was no audible answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think you may need to move a bit closer to the -- well, we'll try that. Sir, I'm going to try to move fairly quickly through some of your background which I hope won't be disputed. As you indicated a few moments ago, you were born on the 4th of November, 1952. As I understand it, you completed training and education in the field of construction technician in 1973. In 1973 and 1974, you completed your military service with the JNA. Let me stop there and ask you, is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Following your service in the JNA, from approximately the 25th of May, 1975, to the 15th of October, 1978, you worked for the parks, essentially what might be called the parks department of the city of Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the period, the 15th of October, 1978, to the 30th of October, 1991, you were an instructor for employment at the district prison in Mostar on Ricinova street; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just because you spent a great deal of your professional life in that position, could you please ever so briefly explain to the Judges what that job involved? When you say instructor for employment at the district prison, what did your job actually involve on a more or less daily basis?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: There was an economic industrial unit at the district prison in Mostar and it had us own estate. Next to that estate, next to that farm, in fact, which was tilled it had orchards. Prisoners who were in prison for more than six months were also obliged to work, at least all of them who were able to work and who were able to leave the prison and who were healthy had to work in enterprises with which I signed agreements or contracts, and that was a measure of re-education. They would leave every morning and return in the afternoon after work. They would spend the night in prison, and that's how it went from day-to-day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, it's already mentioned that you retired then from that position in 1991, October of 1991, and I take it were in retirement for a period of time until approximately mid-1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In July 1992 you joined the HVO, and my understanding, sir, is that you were approached by someone working in the HVO prison system, and because of your background working in prisons you were asked to return once again to the field of prison work in this instance in the Mostar district prison at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And after that time is it correct to say that you then became involved in the actual construction or remodelling a part of the Heliodrom facility to also serve as a prison facility for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just by way of overview, and of course we're going to talk about this in much greater detail the next day or two, so the Judges can put some dates on your involvement and your positions is it correct, sir, that from approximately then the 21st of September, 1992, until the 10th of December, 1993, you were the deputy warden of the Heliodrom prison near Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that from the 10th of December, 1993, until 1 July 1994 you were then the co-commander or co-warden of what was then called the Heliodrom prisoner of war camp?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let's talk briefly about your time during the construction phase of establishing the Heliodrom prison. Can you tell the Judges a little bit how you became involved in that work and what you did during approximately the summer of 1992 to bring that facility into existence.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: When I started talking to the warden of the prison, Mr. Pero Nikolic, he told me to come and see him and help him with his affairs, the work that will be done at Heliodrom, that a military prison would be built for the purpose of separating civilians from the military. Every day after the morning briefing the warden would distribute assignments, and I would go to Heliodrom, to the building that had already been selected as one which would be most easily converted into a prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct to say, sir, that that building, the one you just referred to, is then what became and what will be referred to in the course of your testimony as the "prison building" at the Heliodrom complex?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just while we're on background, sir, and I think the Judges will probably have heard evidence about this, but just to confirm, is it correct that the Heliodrom had been up until that time a JNA military facility and then sometime around June or July of 1992 had been converted and used as an HVO barracks? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, approximately when the Heliodrom prison in this form was opened? When did it actually begin to receive prisoners, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: On the 22nd of September the transfer of military detainees and prisoners of war began.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, if prior to that time, prior to the 22nd of September of 1992, but perhaps earlier in that month, did you have a meeting with Mr. Nikolic, the warden, and anyone else in connection with the opening of the prison and your position or function there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Every morning I would meet with the warden, Nikolic, and receive instructions for my work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've just answered a series of questions that in the mind of a lawyer raised a whole new series of questions, but from what you just told the Prosecutor, you assumed your duties on the 22nd September, 1992, as deputy warden, and at that moment it was a military prison, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when you were appointed deputy warden, did you have a military rank, and were you officially a military man? Because this system of prisons is something that I seem to recognise from my country, although there are certain differences. So I'm just trying to see what questions are appropriate to be asked of you. On the 22nd of September, 1992, when you were appointed deputy warden of that military prison did you have a military rank or a unit -- and/or a unit that you belonged to? Can you specify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 22nd when we transferred to Heliodrom, to the military prison, I did not have any appointment, because at that time only the warden of the prison was appointed and the commander of the prison, and there were shift commanders and guards who were appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But on the 22nd of September you were going to that prison, as you said. Were you paid? Who was paying you? Or were you just working as a volunteer for humanitarian reasons? Tell me, what was your function then, your title on the 22nd September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the salaries that I know of I received through the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were paid by the military police, and you arrived at Heliodrom on the 22nd of September. At that point, was there a document or a verbal order to the effect that you were going to be deputy warden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never received that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A very small, a very short question. You have used the term "warden," and you have used the term "commander." Do they designate the same person? Is it the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I had no appointment of my own, Warden Pusic told me that I may discharge functions and stand in for him. And let me emphasise it was Mile Pusic, because there are several Pusics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you very quickly describe the organisational and administrative structure of the management of that military prison from September 1992 onwards, because I see that you are beginning to -- introducing elements such as that you were not appointed, et cetera. So tell us, who was the warden and who was the deputy. Can you describe it from your memory?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me. I'm really sorry, but I think I may assist with the answer to Honourable Judge Trechsel. The Witness said commander of the security, security commander; however, the word "security" is missing from the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might be allowed to intervene, with all respect. These are all questions that the Prosecution is prepared to answer. We even have a chart of the administrative structure, and I would for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you, prior to arriving or taking up this position which we're going to continue talking about, on the 22nd of September, 1992, can I please direct your attention back a few weeks earlier to the 8th of September, 1992? Did you on that day meet with both Mr. Pero Nikolic, a man you've already described, and also a man named Valentin Coric?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where did you meet with Mr. Coric and Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Nikolic came to fetch me at Heliodrom, and we went to Ljubuski to see Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you understand where particularly in Ljubuski you went to meet Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nikolic told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was the location?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: At Heliodrom and on the way to Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, my question to you, sir, when you met with Mr. Coric in Ljubuski, can you tell the Judges -- I don't want to get too seriously bogged down in this, but do you recall where, what building or location you met with Mr. Coric in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: It was his office in the middle of Ljubuski. The military prison in Ljubuski was later housed in that prison, and that belonged to our company towards the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Judges as best you recall the conversation or what took place during this meeting between Mr. Nikolic, Mr. Coric, and yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic informed Mr. Coric that the works at Heliodrom are being finalised, that the building would soon be ready, and that the transfer would soon be able to take place. In addition to that, Mr. Coric emphasised the importance of that prison that would be named military investigations prison of Herceg-Bosna. And he also explained the purpose of the prison that would exist in the peace -- on the peace side. That's the part that I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall -- you mentioned in response to questions from the President a few minutes ago, that you mentioned the name Mile Pusic. Did Mr. Coric say anything about Mr. Pusic, this Mile Pusic, and what his position would be at the Heliodrom facility at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I remember it. Mr. Coric said that he had selected and found the warden. His name was Mile Pusic. And that man, he was also commander of the 6th Battalion that was deployed within the perimeter of Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, sir, the 6th Battalion, was that a formation of the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO, that had been based in Krusevo?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, during this conversation did your role or function come up in the meeting with Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I was not even mentioned. All the talk was about Mr. Mile Pusic. And Mr. Pero Nikolic was instructed to choose himself commanders of security and shift leaders as well as military policemen who would move to Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, maybe it's a matter of interpretation, but in line 4 of page 21 in English, I see that there is a reference to military investigations prison of Herceg-Bosna, whereas in the French interpretation I did not hear the word "investigations." What exactly did you say in your language, because there are military prisons that are two-pronged, a part that holds military prisoners serving a sentence, but also prisoners in another part who are being investigated. So that particular prison you are talking about, was that also supposed to serve for military investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The full name was Central Military Investigations Prison of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you say that word in the -- in your language again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Central Military Investigation Prison of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, on this point before we come back to the topic of your -- the role you came to play at this time, did you understand based on a conversation with Mr. Coric, and I believe you mentioned this a few moments ago, that this facility at that time would be used to hold, if you will, both military discipline detainees and also prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just for the record and so it's clear, at that particular time in September 1992, is it fair to say that most of the prisoners of war were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mentioned a moment ago if I heard you correctly that Mr. Coric or is somebody had said it would be up to Mr. Pusic, and I won't keep distinguishing between the two, but again this is not the accused in this case but Mile Pusic, would select some of his staff or perhaps all of his staff. Did you -- excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mile Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Could you confirm that the role you took initially at that time was something as an advisor for Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, that's what I would call it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again about family ties. To the best your knowledge, was Mr. Mile Pusic a relative of Mr. Berislav Pusic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. Probably not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, could you also tell us before we move further, at the time that the Heliodrom prison was brought on line, if you will, in September of 1992, what was the approximate capacity? That is, how many prisoners could that facility hold at what might be called full capacity, properly hold?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Five hundred to 520 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, around this time as the prison was opened on the 22nd of September, 1992, did Mr. Coric provide an instruction book or something that was perhaps referred to as house rules on how the prison should be run?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask, please, that the witness be assisted in looking at Exhibit P 00514.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us the number of the binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm -- for the information of those not using e-court, Your Honour, I'm told it's in binder 13 -- bundle 13, excuse me, bundle 13, part 1, which is essentially most of the documents that we'll actually be using in court with the witness. Not all, but most. And they are tabbed as usual for the Judges. So we're talking about 514. My apology for not pointing that out sooner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you have that, sir, and from my vantage point it appears that you do, if you can look at Exhibit 514 in your language, and can you tell the Judges is what you see there the document that was provided by Mr. Coric in September 1992 as the house rules for the Heliodrom prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges, please, for what period of time -- until when do these rules continue to apply at the Heliodrom prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: The rules did not change all the way until the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat this word? We did not understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The house rules did not change.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To make it concrete for our purposes, sir, which we're primarily interested in and perhaps extending in the period late December 1993, early 1994, did these rules, the house rules that are shown in Exhibit 514, did those rules continue to be in effect throughout the period September 1992 to December 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: The house rules of the prison remain the same throughout, although in June there was a minor reorganisation, namely the district prison -- or, rather, the security service was attached to the 5th Battalion of the military police as a platoon of one of its companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, can I ask you just so the record is clear, when you say June, are you now referring to June 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Full, sir, allow me to come to that organisational adjustment in a moment or two. Can you tell us where this book of house rules -- where that was kept and around the Heliodrom prison throughout this time period, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: In the prison building it was accessible to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you confirm to the Judges that a copy of the house rules was in the duty room?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, before moving further into 1993, just to touch on -- we mentioned prisoners of war and Serbs that were being held at that time. Can I just please ask the witness look at Exhibit 677. It's in the same binder, 677.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Before we move on to the next document, sir, I'd like a precision. The Prosecutor showed you the document 514, and the title of that document was "Instructions for the Operation of the Central Military Prison," and I observe that the word "investigation" doesn't appear there, but let's move on. In this the distinction is made between prisoners of war and military prisoners. That's clearly made with a slight nuance. As military prisoners, it refers also to civilians who can be incarcerated who have committed a crime against the military or the army. So this prison seems to be taking in three categories of persons, prisoners of war, soldiers, and civilians. Now, these categories in legal terms, in the administration of a prison was somebody in charge of verifying their status, of checking their status, because as you know a prisoner of war invokes the Geneva Conventions and they have special status. Military men or soldiers who are serving a sentence, whether it be disciplinary or a term in prison from a military court, or a civilian who is incarcerated as a detainee, and now we have a military magistrate. Now, you as the warden, did you deal with these different situations, the different people and different types of person who were in the prison? Did you look at their different status?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as when people came in, those who processed certain military prisoners, it was only them who knew about the crimes and they would be placed in the section of the military prison. Now, when prisoners of war came in, they were put up in another part of the prison. So not together with the soldiers, the military prisoners, but in a separate part. It was physically separate. And then part of the investigating part of the prison and those doing the investigations, they would be alone because at that point in time there was enough room in the prisons. So the prison functioned in the best possible -- under the best possible conditions. There was no overcrowding at the time. All the files and dossiers about the case history of the individuals, it was only people who investigated and interrogated the prisoners who had access to those files. Now, those who had been sentenced as military, they had to spend 10, 15 days in prisons, or however many they were sentenced to, and we knew who those were and when they would be leaving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, if I've understood you correctly, and I think I have, what you're saying is that all the people that were in the prison had a status which allowed them to be placed in the section for prisoners of war, for military prisoners or in the part or investigations and interrogations were conducted by either the military police or the civilian police. Is that roughly what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll come back to that. Mr. Scott, please proceed. We had to make those precisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I can assure the Chamber that when we get later into 1993, we'll pursue that with even greater precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I can -- if you have document 677 in front of you. Can you first of all just confirm for us, there are several references in the first page of the document, the first paragraph and the second paragraph, to the military remand centres in Livno, Mostar, and Tomislavgrad. Can you just confirm that when we talk about the military remand centre in Mostar, at this time this is a reference to the Heliodrom facility?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: An explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: The central military investigation prison, while there was still no conflict going on it was there that we had detainees both from Livno and from other places in Herceg-Bosna who had committed some crimes and were serving sentence, having been found guilty. But the war wasn't on yet at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, when you say the war wasn't on yet, I -- is it correct, sir, can we all understand you to mean that the war between the Croats and Muslims hadn't started yet as of October 1992, at this particular time period? In your view, at least.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: What I want to say is that it was peaceful, peacetime, and that the conditions were ideal at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, this talks about the release of approximately 150 to 200 Serb prisoners of war in October 1992, and this is -- by the way, this is a report dated the 31st of October, 1992, from Mr. Valentin Coric to Mr. Bruno Stojic as chief of the defence department. And did you have any role at the Mostar facility in the release of these Serb prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I remember that these Serb prisoners, I read out their names at the entrance and called them out when they were getting ready to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall the role, very briefly, and we're going to move forward, but can you recall in this particular instance what role the International Committee of the Red Cross, the EU representatives, and UNPROFOR played in the release of these Serb prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: They were present, and most probably they followed the orders to see how they were being applied in the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you've just said that you were present when these prisoners of war, Serb prisoners of war, were released, because you said you were present and you even spoke to them. Now, when you saw them leave, did all those Serbs -- were all those Serbs military men belonging to the ex-JNA, or were there some prisoners of war there who were also civilians, Serb civilians? To the best of your recollections, could you tell us about that? Could you tell us who those prisoners of war were who were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We in the prison, not I but all the people who were in the -- in prison, didn't know exactly who was a prisoner of war and who was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But did somebody know at least? Was there somebody who knew? You said "we." Perhaps you didn't know, but was there somebody who did know, who knew exactly who was who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant at the level of the prison, Mile Pusic and the others below. However, those higher up must have known. Probably they knew. They must have known who were civilians and who about prisoner of war, but at a higher level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as far as the prisoners of war who were released, you can't tell us whether they were all former soldiers or whether there were military men and civilians, Serbs? You're not able to tell us that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't confirm that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us -- I was at -- my question to you was about the EU representatives, the Red Cross, the -- and UNPROFOR. Did you -- was there any similarity that the role those agencies played in the release of Serb prisoners in 1992 to what you then experienced approximately a year later when Muslim prisoners were released from the HVO prisons in 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: As far as I know, I think that's what the situation was. They were just as present as the International Red Cross was present later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Moving forward then, sir. At the end of 1992, in December, did Mr. Coric appoint Stanko Bozic as warden of the Heliodrom prison in place of Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall, please, and can you tell the Judges whether Mr. Coric came to the Heliodrom on the 21st of December, 1992, for the purpose of installing Mr. Bozic as warden?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was anything more formal done at that time about your title or position being perhaps moving from "an advisor," to being a deputy warden?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: No. I remained the way I had been up until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps be just assist us in telling at what point would you -- do you consider that by whatever means or method, de facto, de jure, whatever, that you began to use the title and function as deputy warden of the Heliodrom prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: As I was in Ricinova street, in the District Court, the deputy warden, all this signing and everything, I didn't change that till the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say "the end," what do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Until the appointment as deputy commander of the prisoner of war facility at the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So are you telling the Judges then that in terms -- from a de jure point of view you weren't officially given that title in fact until the end of 1993? De jure, de jure, if you understand that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you -- did the time -- but you continued to work closely with Mr. Bozic going forward from December 1992 and through 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you and Mr. Bozic in fact share a secretary?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the name of the secretary, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Snjezana Cvitanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And during the time period that we're talking about now, and that is as early as December 1992 and the first few months of 1993, was there a man at the facility called Ante Smiljanic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was Mr. Smiljanic's position or function?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: The security commander of the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look at in the bundle that you have in front of you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it's the same bundle, Your Honours, that we've been looking at so far, Exhibit 1711. Bless you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document that appears to be signed by you. I'll ask you to confirm that in a moment - to Bruno Stojic and Valentin Coric dated the 20 -- excuse me, the 23rd of March, 1993. Is it correct, sir, that at the period indicated in this document during the time when Mr. Bozic [Realtime transcript read in error "Coric"] was away you were acting, in fact, as warden of the Heliodrom prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that the dates of that were approximately the 7th of February, 1993, until the 22nd of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who, if anyone, named you or put you in the position of warden during the time that Mr. Bozic was away? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise but there is an error in the transcript. Mr. Scott, on page 32, line 12 to 14, it says that when Mr. Coric was away that the gentleman was acting and so on, signing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. Counsel is correct. The record should reflect -- I don't think it had been in dispute, that it should be when Mr. Bozic was away. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, going back to my question, do you know who it was who named you or put you in the position while Mr. Bozic was away?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: May I give an explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: When on the 7th of February, 1993, Bozic left pursuant to permission from Valentin Coric to go back to his firm and work there where he'd been working before the war, the prison was left without a warden. And then I asked over the phone - Mr. Coric - what was going to happen with the prison. What are we going to do, that somebody had to be appointed to take care of the prison. And he said to me, "Continue working. You, Josip, will report back to me, and Ante Smiljanic will be responsible to me for the prison and for the guards," but that soon a man would be found, someone would be found to perform the function of warden. And when I sent out my reports, I would sign as warden. And then on the 22nd of March, 1993, Mr. Stanko Bozic appeared in the prison. I informed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you're giving us some interesting details, but I'm a little troubled by one point. You said that you called Mr. Coric up on the phone and that he told you to continue working, you, Josip Praljak, to continue doing your work and to send him reports, but that Ante Smiljanic would be in charge of the security in the prison and the guards until a warden had been found.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, as you know, a prison has the number one man who is the warden, the chief, the head, and then the heads of the guards, that's the next level down. Now, on the 7th of February to the 22nd of March were you in charge of questions of security as well, or did your prison function with two authorities, you in charge of logistics, administration, and so on, and Mr. Smiljanic who was in charge of the security and the guards? Can you tell us what it is exactly that you were in charge of and responsible for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the time mentioned here, I was just the person who informed and reported about the events going on in the prison, and that is why I wrote this particular report saying that at that time if anything happened I would be fully responsible. I would take on all material responsibility. Now, my writing, did was that I hadn't been appointed warden myself. And also, when Mr. Bozic returned, he just took over the prison as if he'd never left. So that was the object of my writing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's imagine the situation during the interim period, that a guard, for example, beat a detainee. Let's put that hypothetical. So who would be responsible? Would it be you or Mr. Smiljanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person in that -- who was in that place, in that spot and saw what was going on the I never saw anything like that, nor did anybody ever warn me of any such things and tell me that anything like that was going on at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you as the interim warden, you didn't tour the premises to see what was going on? You didn't talk to the prisoners? You didn't keep informed -- you weren't kept informed about any incidents and exercise all your authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the prison itself is concerned, all the reports would be brought in by Mr. Ante Smiljanic in the morning, and he would inform us of all the events that had happened during the night, as handed over to him by the shift commander, because I worked from 8.00 in the morning until 4.00 p.m. Those were my working hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So you say that Mr. Smiljanic came to report to you on what had happened every day. Now, let's imagine that Mr. Smiljanic told you that guard X during the night had beat detainee Y. What would you have done under those circumstances? Did you have the power and authority to discipline the guard, guard X, take disciplinary measures, or what? What would you have done faced with a situation like that? Now, maybe between February and March nothing like that happened, but let's just take this hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had Mr. Smiljanic informed me, then I would have written a report and sent the report to the crime department or crime prevention department of the military police to investigate the incident and to bring the perpetrators to justice, and all the superior authorities would have been informed about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, your testimony is rather perplexing in portions to me, because if I look at the background, your background as explained to us by the Prosecutor, somebody who is competent, who has ample experience in penitentiary matters, that you worked at Heliodrom for a long time and that you contributing to establishing the organisation in the prison, so you worked for a long time without having any official title. You wrote reports and acted in place of the warden when necessary, and you were aware of hierarchy and the military police and so on. Now, my question is this: Why were you not officially appointed for a long time? Was it because the hierarchy in the military police was such that they did not think you competent enough, regardless of your qualification, or did you have some other secret assignment? Were you on a secret mission given to you by the military police officials that you had to implement without drawing attention to yourself? Or perhaps there was some other reason that you can tell the Chamber of, and that you can explain to us why you were not appointed from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for an answer to the question, the book that was shown a moment ago, there wasn't a post called deputy warden. So I was not able to be assigned that role. The post didn't exist, and I couldn't be appointed to a post that didn't in actual fact exist. But I performed the task in an advisory capacity because I had permission to do that from the warden himself, who was Mile Pusic, and so that's how I introduced myself and that's how I signed my name, although I do think I had a great deal of experience in prison affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To follow up from my fellow Judge's question, which was a very precise question, and I'm not sure that you're replying specifically enough, in February -- let's imagine this: In February, the international community, the ICRC, for example, the European Union or some well-known personage comes to the prison. Let's take that as a hypothesis. Who would go and greet them, greet this high-ranking visitor as being the person responsible in the prison to receive visitors? Would that have been you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as I did do in fact at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's quarter to 4.00. We're going to take a 20-minute break and reconvene at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Praljak, I'd like to move forward, please, from the document that we were just looking at and turning, in fact, back to the question -- some of the questions that the President was raising earlier today. As we move into 1993 and after Mr. Bozic returned as we saw in the last document at approximately the end of March, so we're focusing on that period forward, please, is it correct that under -- at that time you, Mr. Bozic, and Mr. Smiljanic, were you all HVO military police, or did you consider yourself all to be HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And we're going to come at some point very soon to the organisational changes that took place in June, but we're not there yet. Prior to June 1993, is it fair to say that the Heliodrom prison administration was essentially a -- what might be called an independent or self-standing unit?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Bozic was the head of that unit, is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who was Mr. Bozic's superior during that time period?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you said a few minutes ago or earlier this afternoon that around June of 1993 the 5th Battalion of military police was organised, and part of that organisation, the 1st Company, became associated with the Heliodrom prison in some way; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe to the Judges what happen at that time and how that affected the organisation or structure of the Heliodrom prison administration?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: In June the 5th Battalion of the military police was established with Ivan Antic [phoen] as commander. At that time this prison where I, Bozic, Smiljanic, and the guard service worked became attached to one of the companies of that battalion as a Security Platoon. The commander of the company was Mr. Luka Sunjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Several questions about that. During this time and again following up on questions asked by the Judges earlier, did you, though, Mr. Bozic, yourself, Mr. Smiljanic, all continue to be members of the military police, and were you paid your salary from the military police throughout this period?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, in terms of how the Heliodrom prison was actually run on a day-to-day basis, did the involvement or the association with the 1st Company of the 5th Battalion military police have any actual direct impact on the day-to-day structure and operations of the prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Work at the prison continued as before, with the proviso that we addressed Mr. Luka Sunjic, commander of the company, with requests for assistance in logistics, namely to increase the number of policemen so that the security of the detainees would be improved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Praljak, I would like to clarify something. It's perhaps just linguistic. First, and that would be on page 38, line 22, you spoke of a Security Platoon under Mr. Luka Sunjic. Later you speak, on page 39, line 11, of a company. To my military knowledge, you have a battalion, then the company, and the platoon is -- is lower. Now, was this a company or was it a platoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We, the prison, were a platoon, like a platoon, and we belonged to the company led by Commander Luka Sunjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct then that from an administrative and logistics perspective you were treated as a platoon as a -- excuse me, as a platoon of the 1st Company, 5th Battalion military police?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But just to further clarify on this, for instance, can you tell the Judges at any time in 1993 did you ever see Luka Sunjic actually come to the prison, actually come and do any business at the Heliodrom prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I never saw Luka Sunjic at Heliodrom, only at the military police, in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the usher to put something on the ELMO that I will be asking for an IC number for, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can look at that, what's been placed on the ELMO next to you, sir, if you can see that. Sir, can you just look at this drawing and -- which is based on a handwritten diagram that you had shown me, does this -- is this an accurate representation or presentation of the structure of the Heliodrom prison administration for the period April-November 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, Your Honours, Mr. Scott's question intended to ask about the de jure position or the witness's own personal understanding of what the structure is?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour. I'll ask further questions of the witness -- from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just building on the question I put to you a moment ago, sir -- well, several things you've said so far, if I understand you correctly, and, if I don't, I'm sure I'll be corrected. Around June 1993 the prison unit was attached to the 1st Company, 5th Battalion military police for administrative and logistical purposes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then you told us -- also told us a few moments ago that in fact Mr. Sunjic, who is not actually indicated on the chart but the commander of the 1st Company, did I understand you to testify that you never saw Mr. Sunjic come to the Heliodrom, not even one time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I never saw him with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So looking at what's in front of you now and to follow up on counsel's question, does this indicate to you, or does this fairly represent essentially the de facto, if not, in fact, both the de facto and de jure structure at the Heliodrom prison during the period April-November 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I could have an IC number for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document will become Exhibit IC 448.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Mr. Prosecutor. Witness, you say you never saw Mr. Luka Sunjic at the Heliodrom, but he was the commander of the company that had the prison in its jurisdiction. How did he exercise his command over the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For our purposes, for whatever we needed, Mr. Ante Smiljanic would be the person that Bozic and I would go to see in Mostar. We would have a meeting with him, explain what we needed, what kind of assistance, and that's the only kind of meeting we had with him in his office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You just said something that does not quite tally with the schematic that we just saw. You said that Mr. Bozic and Mr. Smiljanic went to see Luka Sunjic. However, if we look at this schematic, we have the impression that the 1st Company of the 5th Battalion had only the commander of the guard to talk to, Mr. Simic, but from what you just said, it seems that we should also make the dotted line -- draw the dotted line towards Mr. Bozic? What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we had our own vehicle as well, for all the requests and for fuel, Mr. Bozic would go himself or send me. I would take a request, fill the tank, and I would also see Mr. Luka Sunjic, or both I and Stanko Bozic would go and see him to deal with logistical matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the other question that arises from this exhibit is that Mr. -- the witness is listed as being deputy warden, a fact that he has consistently denied despite questioning by Mr. Scott for quite some time. So if this is to represent the de jure position, perhaps it does need some clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. If I might. In the course of Mr. Praljak's testimony I think it will be become clear -- I submit that it will become clear that for all practical purposes, I'll use that term, I think arising to the level of de jure but that will be question for argument perhaps later. He did act as deputy warden. The Chamber is going to see document after document that he signed using the term "deputy warden." So I think at the end of the evidence, Your Honours, you will have to make your own determinations as to that. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Just to avoid confusion and to save time, when the previous witness was questioned it was said that the 5th Battalion was established from June, whereas our schematic says April. Maybe there's some confusion here. Maybe we can clarify it because it's completely contrary to what the witness said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If it will assist, Your Honour, I'll try to ask some follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, if we can look at the chart, putting aside for one moment, and I was standing there next to you I might even just put my hand and maybe the usher could simply put his hand over the part that says 1st Company, 5th Battalion military police so we can't see it. Now what we're looking at now would that essentially have been the structure prior to June 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So it was only in June 1993, the only change was - and remove your hand, usher, please - that this association with the 1st Company, 5th Battalion was put into place; is that correct? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: If I can clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: If we take what we see at the beginning, April-November, that I couldn't possibly say exactly whether it was true in April, but I know it was true in June. And if we are looking for an exact date, then it's rather June than April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Certainly for the -- all right. We'll accept that and move forward, because in a very short time the only thing we're going to be talking about is June forward. So I think we can move forward on that basis, Mr. Praljak, and thank you for that clarification. Sir, can I ask you, in terms of the guards at the facility, is it correct to say that the military prison, Heliodrom prison, was under the command of the HVO military police on a 24 hour a day basis?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were there a series of shifts that were staffed by various guard details?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct that sometimes they were 12-hour shifts and sometimes they were 8-hour shifts?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you've already indicated that Ante Smiljanic during this time was the guard commander. Can you tell us, if you can remember, and again if it will assist, if it will make things simpler, I'm happy just to focus primarily on the period June forward, can you tell the Judges who the shift commanders were, if we look again our chart, I'm talking about the level commanders immediately below Mr. Smiljanic during this time period. It may assist the Judges at some point to know who the shift commanders were.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I don't know if I will be able to enumerate them all, but I remember Ivan Zadro, Mario Puce, Ante Buhovac. That's a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can you remember any other names?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Those are the ones I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I might, can you remember a Branko Jedva?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Branko Jedva was also there right at the beginning. I don't know until when, but later he moved to another unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How about Slavko Kozul?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Slavko Kozul too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what about Pero Marijanovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: He came later but he was deputy commander for security to Ante Smiljanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection -- and when you say he came later, how much later? And -- well, let me ask it this way: Approximately what time in 1993 he came?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I think it was around March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you recall any others or to the best of your knowledge would the names we've just listed in the last few minutes be the shift -- excuse me -- the persons who were the shift commanders during this period?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, we just mentioned those shift commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Very well. If I could have the usher's assistance to show you another document that will be marked as IC -- I'll ask for an IC number in a moment. If you can put that on the ELMO, please. Sir, is it correct that when we -- when I met with you in the last day or two I showed you this diagram without any of the red lettering on it, and I asked you, if you could, to identify the principal buildings or facilities that made up the Heliodrom prison in 1993, and is what we're looking at the ELMO now, is that the drawing, and are the red markings on that, is that your handwriting and your markings?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Since you've written, of course, in your own native language, I'll just look at -- can you just take us through -- you can start anywhere you'd like, but if you would just take us through the various locations you've made? What you've done in all instances is drawn an arrow and given us a name. If you can just take us through those and tell us the location you've marked, and lastly we'll ask for the translation from our helpful interpreters. Perhaps starting on the left side, up, Zatvor, what is that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: This is the building of the prison or, rather, the building that was purposefully made as a building, the central military investigations prison that we referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, when we talk about that building and the prison building, is that the building that you helped construct to convert to a prison in August-September 1992? Is that what you're referring to as the Zatvor?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps you could then continue on around the chart, perhaps clockwise, and tell us what else you've marked.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: This small structure just a metre away from the building of the prison housed the administration where Bozic, I, and Stjelenac [phoen] had their offices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, did you have your own office or did you share an office with somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a big space, so I had my own office as did Bozic as well as Njezinac [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you had your own office. Did you have a telephone set with a separate telephone line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
