utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only Snjezanac [phoen] Cvitanovic had a telephone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you did not have a telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We would answer calls in telephones in Snjezanac Cvitanovic's office both Bozic and I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you replaced Mr. Bozic, did you take over his office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't need to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So how did you manage with the telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only Snjezanac Cvitanovic had a telephone set. I would go to her office and make a telephone call. It was the office next door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it somebody called from outside, for instance, from the defence ministry, from the SECR -- ICRC or a journalist or anybody, how did you answer calls?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Snjezana would answer the call and she would summon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the secretary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the secretary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you could then continue on around. There's a building marked "Skola." What is that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: The school was this part of the building that was used when people were brought in who could not fit into the building of the prison, and then they were put up in the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges if you know approximately -- when was the first time that the school building was used to hold prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was on the 30th of June or the 1st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then continuing on there's another relatively large, dark building or block that appears to be labelled "sports hall," is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can I ask you a similar question? Can you tell the Judges, please, when was the first time that the sports hall was used to house -- by the HVO to house prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: When the building of the school became full, then the door of that hall was opened and people started to be accommodated there. That means in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then if I can ask you to look at the red writing on the lower part of the chart toward the left edge, lower left edge, can you tell us what that information indicates? And it's an arrow -- appears to be an arrow going back towards the Zatvor, the prison building. What do you indicate here?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: What's indicated here is that Ante Smiljanic as commander of security had had his office in the prison building where shift commanders and guards were both stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I have an IC number, Your Honour, for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will become Exhibit IC 449.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I could have the usher's assistance to now hand the witness or -- yeah, than the witness or put on the ELMO for him a photograph, an aerial photograph which I'll ask him to make markings on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can, I'm going to ask you to -- if you can see and mark the same locations on this photograph, the same locations that you marked on the diagram that we were looking at just a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you want me to draw this in?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, please. You can do it the same or you can draw an arrow and -- you can draw a red line or arrow and the name or however you'd like.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that the prison building, what you just marked as Zatvor?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Go ahead, please. Perhaps if you can -- can you show us where the administrative building was located that you and Mr. Bozic and the secretary were located in? Where was the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you also mark the Skola, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can I ask you finally to mark the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, I -- I think the procedure -- I assume that the President would like us to follow would be if you would cut your name initials on that and today's date, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Place your initials there and put the date on the photograph. You can put your initials on the white margin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the date, and it is the 26th of February, 2007.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. An IC number, please, registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, IC 450.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may -- if I may add a question. Witness, you have put the flash which goes to the sports hall so that it is between practically two buildings. Is it between the left-hand building which is a bit higher or the right-hand building which is a bit lower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lower one. The lower one is the sports hall or halls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's right next to that other building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so the record may --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so the record might be clear in the future, sorry, is it correct that it appears that one of the red arrows you draw -- that you drew a moment ago comes down to, just looking at the picture, would be the upper right corner of that building, the roof of that building; is that correct? Maybe you just want to circle it. If there's any dispute, maybe you can just circle the whole building which you're saying is the sports hall. Yes, excuse me, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think between the diagram and the drawing hopefully Your Honours will be satisfied. I'm sure others can follow up. Thank you, usher, that completes the use of those particular items.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, we understand all the better because we were in the locality ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's true. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask if it's correct that during the time period roughly at least -- and it may have been true earlier, it may have been true later, but I'm simply trying to focus our attention for purposes of the record. During the period January through November of 1993 there would be a morning meeting in Mr. Bozic's office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I think you said a few minutes ago earlier today that Mr. Bozic, yourself, and the secretary worked -- the approximate hours of your workday were from 8.00 in the morning until 4.00 in the afternoon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: While the various guard shifts or details would be there on a 24-hour a day basis?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that at the morning meeting in Mr. Bozic's office, Mr. Smiljanic would report to Mr. Bozic about any matters that had happened since 4.00 the previous afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you attend these meetings, sir, by the way?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: If it was necessary. I didn't always attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was there any particular arrangement or procedure by which Mr. Bozic would give you any particular task or assignments on a daily or a weekly basis?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: When there was something I needed to do then he would give me the assignment to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, this morning meeting where you reported to Mr. Bozic about the events that took place after 4.00 p.m. and until 8.00 in the morning, you said you took part in that type of meeting, in those meetings. Now, who reported to Mr. Bozic? Who would make the report to Mr. Bozic? Was it Mr. Smiljanic who would tell him what had happened? So who reported orally to Mr. Bozic? Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Smiljanic as the security commander would report every morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, if Mr. Smiljanic said that such-and-such a detainee was ill or something and that he required help during the night, would Mr. Bozic ask questions in order to gain more information about what had happened and on the report tabled to him? And you yourself, too, or did you just sit back with your hands folded and just listen to what was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If somebody was sick, then there was an infirmary in the prison, and that infirmary was staffed by doctors. Now, in the barracks itself there was a dispensary so that aid could be given at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But let's take a hypothesis. Let's imagine that in the middle of the night a detainee is taken seriously ill, and he was taken to the infirmary and he dies. Now, at that point in time, would one report to will Bozic about what had happened? And, if so, would Mr. Bozic ask questions about the state of health, why the detainee died, and so on and so forth? And did you yourself take part in any events of that kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not take part, but Mr. Bozic, having received information like that, would intervene straight away. He would write an account. He would call his subordinates, and he would go to the infirmary himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask you a more precise question. During the time that you were there, were there ever any detainees who died in prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember of a single case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like -- I would like to ask for a precision. You said that you attended the meeting if necessary. Can you explain to us under what circumstances it was considered necessary that you attend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I was to receive an assignment to do something on that particular day, then Mr. Bozic would call me and inform me of that task or assignment, and he would have given me the assignment to carry out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A follow-up question: We know that the ICRC came to visit the Heliodrom and that some internationals came as well. Now, in order to prepare for this visit was there a meeting in the morning saying that everybody should be prepared, the detainees, that everything should be in order, clean, and so on? So did you have a working meeting in order to prepare a visit by some international organisation of this kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no preparations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You prepared nothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only explanation I can give is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What explanation? Who did the explaining?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to the International Red Cross and their visit, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead, explain this to us. How did you go about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was an International Red Cross visit while I was in prison. This was in February or March 1993. The ICRC told us that they were going to visit, and I received them. I welcomed them and took them to the prison. And I said -- I told the guard service that they should allow the International Red Cross to tour the prison themselves without any guards being present, that they should be allowed to talk to everybody, to the detainees. After that, once they had carried out their visit, they would come to see me in the office and talk to me about their visit. After that, after the visit, I would write out a report, and I would inform Valentin Coric, the head, about it. I would tell him of their comments, what they had noticed, their complaints, objections, and also the good things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm sure we'll come back to that question in due course. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, just to finish up on some of these background matters that will then help us for the remainder of your testimony, and since it may come up from time to time, when we talk about the -- when we talk about the Heliodrom, is it -- is it accurate to say the Heliodrom itself was a much larger complex? When people say "the Heliodrom," it's a much larger complex than just the prison facilities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, for instance, if we still had the aerial photograph in front of us that we were looking at a few minutes ago, there would be many parts of that facility that were not considered part of the prison, or not the Skola, or not the sports hall, or not the prison building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us during -- again, if I can focus your attention as much as possible, please, on 1993, and I'm now talking about the Heliodrom in its wider meaning, not the prison but the entire facility, can you tell it us, if you can recall, which HVO units were barracked or headquartered or located at the larger overall Heliodrom facility?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: At the Heliodrom there was the 3rd Brigade of the HVO, and the Bruno Busic regiment was there of the HVO. And also there were units -- well, I don't know what their names were, but they were call the Jukic men. I assume that they took their name from the commander, Juka Prazina. And the Tutici, which I assume were Mladen Naletilic, Tuta's men, or Andabak, as the commander, his men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just for the record when we're looking at page 57 in the transcript, line 2, when you said "Jukic men," could we better understand that to be Juka's men?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The Jukici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A precision about the units. To your knowledge, were there or were there not units belonging to the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never saw anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In reference to -- you mentioned Tutici, Tuta's men. Did your hear there was a unit at the Heliodrom called the ATs -- excuse me, the ATG Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: ATG Baja Kraljevic was later on. It was only later on that we learnt that they had their headquarters at Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And for the record if the Chamber's not heard that abbreviation previously and I don't recall, ATG stands for anti-terrorist group, please. I can see they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir, for the record?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, were this -- with these structures and other background pieces of information in mind, I would like to direct your attention now specifically to the 9th of May, 1993. When you had the meeting with Mr. Bozic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. We talked of units, and when you say units, materiel, equipment, and so on comes to mind straight away. Now, we had a witness who told us something about that, so I'd like your own opinion and your own testimony to receive confirmation or to refute what he said. Within the Heliodrom compound, did you see with your very own eyes any tanks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not a single tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not a single tank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if one of the detainees said that he saw a tank, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what he saw, but I did not see any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there was one, for example, would you have seen it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not from the prison, no. Or near the prison either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in the compound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's a broad area. I never went round the whole compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me narrow my question down. If I take this hypothesis, that a tank fired from the compound, would you have heard it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it fired and if it existed, and if I was there from 6.00 in the morning until 4.00 -- until 2.00 -- or, rather, 4.00 in the afternoon ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness give an answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if it had shot beforehand -- you didn't sleep there, did you? You didn't sleep on the premises. You weren't there during the night between 4.00 p.m. and 6.00 a.m. Where were you? Where did you spend that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My family was located at a place called Siroki Brijeg, which is perhaps 20 kilometres and perhaps more, 25 kilometres, along the macadam road which I had to take every time, and that's where I spent time with my wife and children, that's where I was, so that it isn't possible to hear it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you correctly, at around 4.00 p.m. every day you would leave, and you wouldn't return until the next morning to attend those famous 8.00 morning meetings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what about the weekend, Saturday and Sunday? Were you there or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now at the level of the prison command, the warden, you, the guards commander, was there always somebody permanently there, that ensured permanence? If a problem arose, an invasion, an attack on the prison, who would be able to alert the authorities, the central authorities, so was there a permanent presence there? Were any one of you there at any one time, because there would have had to have been somebody responsible. So was there somebody there in the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The shift commanders were there round the clock, 24 hours in the prison. The prison was never left without security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And was there a timetable with who was on duty, the name of the officer on duty, the person responsible who -- on Saturday and Sunday, a timetable from such-and-such an hour until such-and-such an hour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The orders and timetable was compiled by Ante Smiljanic for his guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A little question just to be precise. You have -- at the beginning you have said that you worked from 8.00 a.m. to 4.00 p.m., and that was also what the president based his last question. But in between, and it can be found on page 59 at lines 6 and 8, you seem to have said that at least sometimes you worked from 6.00 a.m. to 2 p.m. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, from 8.00 to 4.00. Perhaps I might have misspoken. I might have made a slip of the tongue, but what I meant to say was from 8.00 a.m. to 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In February, March, when you were the interim warden, on the weekend, Saturday and Sunday, you weren't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if a problem arose could they call you at home to tell you about what was going on, if they needed to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because you had a telephone at Siroki Brijeg, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if we could go back now to the 9th of May, 1993. Can you tell the Judges whether Mr. Bozic reported any particular information at the morning meeting on that day as to what would happen later that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: At the morning meeting, Mr. Bozic said that during the day there would be a large group coming in of detainees. He did not say what kind of detainees or who or anything like that. And he told Ante - that is, Smiljanic - to prepare the guards and to step up the number of guards for them to be able to take in the incoming people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was anything said by Mr. Bozic around this time whether the regular prison staff would be doing the intaking, intake, taking these people in, or would somebody else be handling that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: On the occasion Mr. Bozic said -- well, one hour later, at about 9.00, that two civilians would be arriving who would take over part of the job of taking in the new arrivals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of these individuals or any others that joined them at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Biljana Nikic came, and Marko Bevanda, too, and they introduced themselves. They said they were in charge of the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did they indicate to you from what organisation or agency or authority they came?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they said that they had come there from the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees and that their boss at the time who knew about this and sent them was Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you happen to recall, if you do, because it may assist us later, do you happen to recall the first name of this Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I know he was in charge of the displaced persons and refugees attached to the ministry as the number-one man for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And can you tell the Judges then what you and those around you on -- later that morning, what did you actually see happening at the Heliodrom prison? Who was coming? What was did you see?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: That morning when they started to arrive, women, children, and men were coming in, women with children of various age groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you able to observe and can you tell the Judges, if you can, what the ethnicity or from what nation or people these persons were from, the people who were coming to the Heliodrom on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: They were Muslims. In the words of Biljana Nikic and Marko Bevanda, they had been expelled -- sorry, displaced from the town that was on the front line, so that they could be accommodated and protected there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It may seem obvious to you, sir, but when you say "from the town," which town are you talking about now?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I don't know, because I was not in town, and I did not even know about the conflict. I just saw those people and heard about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, either later on the 9th of May or the next day or two thereafter, on the 10th of May, or the 11th of May or the 12th of May, did you ever learn any information as to where these Muslim people were coming from?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Since they were men, women, and children, it was clear that they were from Mostar, from the area of combat activities, and I didn't inquire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you observe any of these people carrying personal belongings as they arrived?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Judges how you felt and what your reaction was to seeing these men, women, and children arriving at the Heliodrom prison during those days, the 9th, 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: It was an ugly picture. No matter how people were accommodated after being displaced, it was ugly to see them in that building which, after all, was meant to be a prison, and it was a harrowing sight to see women and children behind bars. And that was filmed by cameras, by reporters. It was difficult to watch that, so I didn't go out there much, and I didn't appear in front of the reporters either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you saw those civilians, including women and children, arrive. You've just said that they were put up in a facility that was meant to be a prison. Who decided to put them up there, because in this vast complex there must have been other possibilities? There was a gym. There were other structures. Why put them in the building that was meant to be a prison? Wasn't it possible to put them up elsewhere in this huge complex?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't answer that question. I think only Mr. Stanko Bozic, who was then warden, could answer it. And Marko Bevanda and Mrs. Biljana Nikic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you didn't play any role at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was inside. I didn't go out once in all those days while that lasted. I was in my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And why didn't you go out to learn the news, to face this situation that was, after all, rather extraordinary, seeing all these people, civilians, in a military installation? It was a novelty. Didn't you want to find out more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't want to go out, because it was not in the jurisdiction of either the prison or Stanko Bozic or myself, but the people who had come to that sector. And also because on the first day a woman met me at the entrance and said, "Can you give me some bread for my child?" I simply couldn't stand it. I went back inside. Marko Bevanda and Biljana Nikic were there, who were supposed to take care of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would have a lot of questions to ask you about that, but I don't want to impinge more upon the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in this regard, and perhaps as we look at some of the documentation some additional details may answer some of the Judge's questions, hopefully, if I can ask you to look at Exhibit P 02260. It should be in the same binder that we've been working in, I think. Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Document title at least in the English translation, Official Note, dated the 10th of May, 1993, apparently signed by Stanko Bozic. Above that there are three names indicated, Stanko Bozic, Josip Praljak, Snjezana Cvitanovic, and there are also handwritten -- well, there's also what appears to be signatures or handwriting next to those. Is -- the handwriting next to the name Josip Praljak, is that yours?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us if you know what led Mr. Bozic to prepare the report and why did all they of you sign this particular document?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Bozic wrote this document for one reason. As people were coming in, Mr. Berislav Pusic started calling. So he received those phone calls asking him to release people -- or, rather, to convey to Biljana and Marko Bevanda the names of people who should be released from the prison or, rather, that admission centre. To make it more precise, since the distance between Heliodrom and Berislav Pusic was great and in order for the releases to be legally valid and all these messages to Biljana Nikic and Marko Bevanda to be in due form, he made this Official Note, citing me and Mrs. Snjezana Cvitanovic as witnesses, confirming that Mr. Berislav Pusic did in fact say that on the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who did you understand Mr. Berislav Pusic to be as of the 9th of May, 1993? What position, if any, did he hold in the Mostar area, and what can you tell the Judges about him at that time, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I know Mr. Berislav Pusic as an official of the military police from Mostar, and at that time he worked in the administration of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know at that time -- when I say that time I mean the 9th of May or the days thereafter, again the 10th or 11th what have you, did you come to know why it was that Mr. Pusic had this role in calling your office and indicating that certain persons should be released?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: As he was an official of the military police, he had the powers to do that without me giving any thought to who those individuals were. Mr. Josip Marcinko, also called -- Mr. Zvonko Vidovic, and they also got some people released, although in smaller numbers. I believed it was an agreement between them as the criminal investigation service, and I thought it was their right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And approximately how long did this process continue of both people being brought to the prison and people being released pursuant to these telephone calls?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I cannot say precisely, but I think that within five or six days all the people who had arrived were released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You signed a document on the 10th of May. We see your name, the name of the secretary, and Mr. Bozic. It's a rather unusual document in itself. You were not a novice in matters of the prison. You had already worked in the civilian sector administrating penitentiary institutions. You said that after the MOS attack on town those civilians had been brought to Heliodrom. So far so good. At that moment, Mr. Pusic calls to get some of them released. Very well, but why did you find it necessary to draw up this document? For what purpose? To protect you in the future? Or to indicate to the military police hierarchy that you had obeyed orders? There must have been a purpose. You declared that you will speak the whole truth. Could you please explain the purpose of this document, because Mr. Bozic made you co-sign it. He didn't take just anybody. He took the deputy, because you were on record as the deputy. Why did you co-sign it, to protect yourself, or for what reason? Because every signature implies some responsibility. It entails some consequences, and you must know that since you worked in prisons. Explain to us, please, why you signed this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not write this document. It was written by Mr. Stanko Bozic. He knows why he wrote it. And I know that I was present throughout that time in one office, because our office was being used by Mr. Marko Bevanda, and we were together all the time in Snjezana's office. In my opinion, Mr. Stanko Bozic was trying to protect himself. And in this case I was just present there, because I would also answer some of those calls. I received some of those calls by Berislav Pusic instructing us to release some people. Snjezana did and Mr. Bozic did too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you said you answered those calls. That means you talked to Berislav Pusic on the phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He would just read out the names. I would write them down and hand them over to Biljana Nikic and Marko Bevanda. We would just hand the lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when he read out those names it was an order that was not subject to any challenge. You only had to execute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was so extraordinary about saying that civilians needed to be released? That kind of order was the most normal under the circumstances. And if you say Mr. Bozic wanted to protect himself, protect himself from what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I couldn't answer that. I tried to explain earlier and I can repeat it. It's possibly because it was all done by telephone, because the same day a report would be written by the people whom Mr. Berislav had released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, during the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. The last thing you have said according to the record, "it's possibly because it was all done by telephone, because the same day a report would be written by the people whom Mr. Berislav had released." That is probably not what you wanted to say. It would be strange if those who are released would write a report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not the people but Mr. Stanko Bozic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as these released -- did these releases then begin happening at some volume? I mean, are we talking about one or two, or are we talking about hundreds?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: By telephone, smaller groups of people would be dictated, five to 10, sometimes individuals only.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you this before I ask you to look at a couple of documents. When people would be -- well, let's -- were people in fact released pursuant to Mr. Pusic's request? That is, we've heard about the request, but did prisoners actually walk out or leave the complex? Were they released based upon Mr. Pusic's authorisation? Or did they --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: They were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when they were released did they simply walk out on their own two legs, or did someone come and collect them, or how did that work?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: No. At that time one couldn't just walk out. They were always escorted out and admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Because of the numbers of releases that were being done, can you tell the Judges, was some sort of a form or a standard written document prepared that would be executed when various people would be authorised for released -- and released?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look in your bundle at Exhibit P 02278. And if you have that, sir, can I simply ask you, is that representative of the type of document that you saw being prepared around the 9th, 10th, 11th of May, around that time, in connection with the release of people who had been held at the prison facility?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you next to look at 2285?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. Witness, you signed a document that we've just seen where it is said that civilians were going to Heliodrom follow a MOS attack. That is understandable. The desire was to protect the civilians and shelter them. But in this document I see the addressee is the chief of the crime prevention service. Why? Why inform the chief of the crime prevention service that three members of the Baralija family were released? It's either because these people were being sheltered from combat activities or the chief of the crime prevention service was alerted to their presence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only suppose we had no one else to send our reports to, only the crime prevention service chief, or the chief of the military police, who is our superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that -- in that regard, sir, if I can direct your attention to the next document in your bundle, which is 2285. Document signed by Mr. Bozic or at least bearing his name dated the 11th of May, 1993. This indicates -- appears to indicate that a person named Jugo was released at the intervention of Mr. Berko Pusic and Mr. Valentin Coric. Can you tell us, if you know, what role Mr. Coric played in having these people released on the 9th, 10th, 11th of May?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: As for these releases, I would not like to comment because I really don't know. I believe it is a rare occasion to see such reports where Mr. Valentin Coric took part, but I suppose Mr. Stanko Bozic would know, because he co-signed it. He signed it, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, one of the things we hope to accomplish with this witness in the course of his testimony is to confirm that the documents that we're looking at are just a few representative documents but in fact there's a large number, and that's why there are other large binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it correct that, and didn't you have a chance to review in the past day or so a number of the same documents released from the Heliodrom 9th, 10th, and 11th of May and following? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to turn to the next document, which is Exhibit P 02315. Sir, this is a document dated the 11th of May, 1993. It ultimately lists approximately, I think, 106 individuals. Can I please direct your attention to the upper right quadrant of the first page. Do you see any handwriting on that document that is yours?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it your handwriting that says: "13 May 1993, as per order of Berko Pusic, nobody can release," underline "release," "persons's whose names are circled." "Josip Praljak" signed; is that correct? And on the language, the original version in your own language, are there a number of names that go on throughout the 106 names? Are their various names that are circled?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I think in the English version, Your Honour, the number has been underlined. So number 3, number 4, number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can I just ask you to confirm, is number -- is the person number listed as number 3, is that person circled?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just one more as an example. Person number 7. Is that -- in your list, is it circled?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, did you get this information from Mr. Pusic - excuse me - on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So can the judges understand correctly then that you were on the telephone with Mr. Pusic, and he was telling you to go through this list and circle the names of persons who should not be released?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges usually always understand in the proper way, but perhaps -- you can't assume that we understand incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand the point. Let me restate my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, is that what happened, that you were on the telephone with Mr. Pusic and he was telling it you which of the names on this list to circle? Or if it happened some other way, tell it us.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, the circled individuals -- well, I don't circle people like this. But as this was in 1993, after all, I think that this document was brought to me and that I put arrows for the people as it says here and just wrote "Remain," or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps the interpreters could assist us. If we can put the original language version on the ELMO so that the interpreters can see it. In the English version the word is interpreted "encircled." I maybe it's a mistranslation. If we could just take it out of his binder, perhaps, in the B/C/S and put it on the ELMO so the interpreters can see it. 2315. 2315. If it's a matter of dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask, please, the assistance of the language -- one the language booths, if you could read out -- if someone could interpret what is written in the Croatian language here and read that out to what -- your interpretation of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The simplest thing would be, Witness, for you to read out the sentence written in handwriting, handwritten, in your own language, and as you're reading it out the interpreters can interpret. What does it say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "According to the orders of Mr. Berko Pusic, the circled individuals cannot be released by anybody." "Encircled."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And going back to what -- your testimony a moment ago -- so are you telling us then, please -- either way, just tell us as best you can recall, please, did you receive the document with the names already circled, or did you circle them as you were receiving information from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: As I know my own handwriting, I don't think I circled them, whereas I did write what it says next to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't want to intervene before, but Mr. Scott is sort of organising the scenario, whereas I think we should allow the witness to say how this note came about, how he encircled the names or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exactly the question I just put, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as far as you remember tell us how all this came about. How were you taken -- how did you come to be -- how did you come to write this in your own hand and sign it? And how the names were circled, could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document, which is signed at the end by Dr. Ante Kvesic, the commander of the regional war hospital, this is a list of his workers and their families. On this list is Mr. Berko, as it says -- Mr. Berko said that the persons encircled cannot be released by anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To summarise the situation as far as I understand it, the doctor who signed this document indicated that a number of individuals who worked for him in his services, the internal medicine services or pulmonology or gynaecology or whatever, that they were at Heliodrom, and then he explains that these people were taken from their apartments and taken away from their apartments. He doesn't say to Heliodrom, but one understands it was to Heliodrom. And then he provides a list. Now, a priori we can think that this -- one could think that this list was compiled so that these people could be released, because since they work in the medical department their presence is necessary for the public hospital to continue functioning. And it seems that on the basis of what you're telling us that Mr. Pusic has launched an appeal and says that on that list there are persons that should not be released, that is to say number 3, 4, 5, et cetera. So is that what happened? Is that how it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to say this: I've looked through the list and I noticed something. I noticed that, for example, under number 74, Djudja Dzemal is the name under 74, a doctor who was still working in Mostar to this day, was never in prison, because I would see him in Siroki where he lived at my cousin's place. So I can't tell you much about this list. I can't tell you much about all these people on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Mr. Praljak. You were speaking of your cousin's place. One of your cousins is present in this room. Was it this cousin or was it another cousin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was another cousin, Grbesic Nikola, who lives in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of what you said, wouldn't this be a recapitulation of the people who were taken away from their apartments but without all of them being in Heliodrom? And here you quoted the example of number 74 who was never at Heliodrom. Would that be an explanation of this list? You're nodding, but will you say yes? Da, in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't explain it any other way, because here the names 3, 4 and 5, Dr. Hadziomerovic, for instance, also a doctor from Mostar, and this is his family, another well-known doctor, it says should remain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How come Mr. Pusic is saying that these people should not be released, whereas they weren't there in the first place? So couldn't you say, or Mr. Bozic say, that those people weren't in fact there in the first place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all the people on the list, the ones who are circled or not, we didn't know whether they were in prison or not. It was the people who listed them who knew and who took care of them. This is just a list of names circled. But whether they were there or not I can't say. I gave you an example of one man who I knew was not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you've given us a plausible explanation. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I note -- I note the time, Your Honour, but perhaps we should take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I didn't see that time was getting on. Let's take a break and reconvene at five past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, before we move forward from this particular series of documents, could I just ask you, you've now made several references to contact with Mr. Pusic and people being released on Mr. Pusic's authorisation. Can you explain to the Judges, please, why you and Mr. Bozic and others apparently followed Mr. Pusic's instructions? Did you consider not -- not doing what he was, according to this evidence, telling you to do?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: We followed his instructions, the instructions of Mr. Berislav Pusic, because he was in the administration of the military police, working in the crime investigation department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you consider him to be your superior for these purposes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: He wasn't directly superior to us, but he did have the right as somebody in the military police administration crime department to issue orders to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look the next at Exhibit P 02321. It should be the next one in your bundle, please. Now, this document appears to have been prepared for the signature of Mr. Bozic, but is it correct, sir, it's -- that you're the one that in fact signed it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall whether this person named Simunovic came and actually collected these people, or is that what this document would indicate?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, to the left of your signature do we understand correctly that on picking up and collecting this individual or these individuals Mr. Simunovic signed the document? Is that how it worked?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look at 2368. And once again is that actually your signature on the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if we understand the document correctly, then in this instance - excuse me - it was Mr. Zelenovic [sic] who collected these people?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is Mr. Zelenovic [sic] a prominent attorney in Mostar? Perhaps I'm mistaken, but if I am, I'm sure you'll correct me.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: On the document that I'm looking at there's Predrag Leventic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And down at the end of the document there appears to be a place where Mr. Nuzimevid -- Muslinovic signed the document. My apology. I've been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's not on the -- I apologise, Your Honour. It's not on the original document, which I had noted previously but I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you -- can you tell the Judges, did you see any pattern of the people who were being released, any types of people, any groups of people or can you assist the Judges at all with what you saw?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I don't think there was any selection from among the people. I think that he knew the people, Mr. Predrag Leventic, that is, and he asked them to be taken out, and Mr. Berko allowed that to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps this is a good moment. There's a general mistake on page 79, line 1. It says that these people were collected. It says who collected these people. Now, from the document it would emerge that they be released. So quite the opposite. Not collected but released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I'm the source of the confusion, I apologise. What I'd asked Mr. Praljak earlier today is that when the people were released did they simply walk out on the street or did someone come and collect them, in that sense, and that's the -- pick them up. So sorry, that's another terminology. I'll ask the witness again, if it assists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you go back to the line of counsel's question, if I can ask you to go back to 2321, the document we were looking at a moment ago. I think you testified to this, but in light -- again, in light of counsel's question. On 2321, yes, when -- it bears the -- the -- excuse me, the signature there of Mr. Simunovic, and over that at least it's translated, it says "Taken over by." Did you understand that to mean that it was Mr. Simunovic who picked up the people being released?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. And he signed for them, signed for having taken them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Could I ask you next, please, to look at Exhibit P 02853. Do you have that? It may be several down. You'll have to find the number. 2853. If you have that, sir, is this a report by Mr. Bozic to Mr. Valentin Coric dated the 19th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do we understand correctly that the document says this is the report for the month of May 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, was that the practice that Mr. Bozic would make a report for each month to Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking at the first sentence -- well, let me -- before I ask you did you ever -- did you or Mr. Bozic or any of you at the Heliodrom prison during this first part of May, first half of May or so, 1993, did you ever come up with a number of how many people were brought into the Heliodrom around the 9th, 10th, 11th of May in the way that you've described us -- to us this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Records of arrival were kept by Marko Bevanda and Biljana Nikic. And if I might be allowed to say, since Bozic wrote this report, that it went through -- that 1.820 displaced persons went through the institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you accept that as a fair number or at least estimate of how many people did in fact go to the institution at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: There's no reason for Mr. Bozic to think that up, to invent that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And can I ask you, please, to go next to Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before I do, Your Honour, I'm told that the next exhibit -- if we go to private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, now I'm directing your attention specifically to the 30th of June, 1993, and in a similar fashion to when I asked you about the 9th of May, do you recall during the morning meeting on the 30th of June whether Mr. Bozic reported that something would be happening that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: That morning Mr. Bozic said that a large group would be arriving at Heliodrom. He didn't explain anything. He didn't say who or why, just like he did on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did he provide any more information about the identity of the people who would be - excuse me - arriving?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell us anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what happened later that day and in the days that followed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: They started arriving. Large groups began to arrive, groups of people who came to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were these groups similar to those that had come on the 9th and 10th of May or were they different?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: No. There were no women and children, just men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were you able to determine at the time or did you come to know the ethnicity of the men who were being brought to the Heliodrom prison on the 30th of June and thereafter?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: They were Muslims, Muslim men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you sometime after those days in early -- well, early July 1993, did you ever come to have a number -- we were looking at a number a few minutes ago for May. Did you ever come to have a number of how many Muslim men were brought into the Heliodrom in the first part of July 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: We never established the number of people who arrived, because that job, the job of taking them in and registering them, registering those who were arriving, was done by 10 to 12 employees of the MUP, of the military police, of the SIS, with Zvonko Vidovic at its head.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Before I come, follow up on those particular answers, when you received prisoners around this -- "you" being the Heliodrom, did it come to the point that the prison, what we've called the prison building, came to capacity, was filled to capacity?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that as you told us earlier this afternoon that it was on this occasion that -- where the school was first used to house prisoners and then the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Judges more what was said or understood by you as to the role of Mr. Zvonko Vidovic in doing the intake or reception of these people who were coming to the Heliodrom prison at this time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Zvonko Vidovic informed Mr. Stanko Bozic, and I was present, that all the registration and taking over of the people who had arrived would be carried out by his people and that they would compile a complete list of the people brought in, which list would be handed over to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was any explanation offered to you or to Mr. Bozic, and you said you were present, as to why this different group of people would be involved in this process as opposed to the regular staff at the prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: He didn't provide an explanation. He just took it upon himself to do that because he had the authority to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you, please, to look at exhibit, in your bundle, 3040. Sir, can you tell us by looking at this document, which appears to be dated on the top of the first page the 30th of June, 1993. Does this appear -- well, can you tell us what that document is, if you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: This is a document compiled by one of the employers -- employees from the team led by Zvonko Vidovic, and this can be seen at the end of the document, and that person was Stjepan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges -- I didn't ask you. Perhaps you can tell us a little more about who Zvonko Vidovic was and what position he held as of the end of June, early July 1993.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Zvonko Vidovic was a criminal investigations officer in the military police. I don't know exactly when he was appointed chief of the crime investigations service in the administration of the military police, but it was around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was he -- when you say chief of criminal investigations, was that a like a department or a particular section of the military police administration?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you know or can you tell us from either because of direct knowledge or because of your knowledge of the structure of the military police administration who was Mr. Vidovic's superior? As a department head, who did he report to?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: The chief of the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who was the chief of military police administration in July 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I think it was Mr. Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you or Mr. Bozic ever raise with Mr. Vidovic whether these lists were adequate or appropriate, provided you with the information you needed to manage these people?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: We didn't have any information, so that Mr. Bozic made our internal list of detainees so that he could order meals and food.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall how long it was before Mr. Bozic obtained -- prepared these separate lists, the lists separate from Mr. Vidovic and his group prepared?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: It was a long time before Mr. Vidovic, after being warned by Mr. Bozic, submitted these lists. Until then we didn't have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Several hours ago the President was asking you questions about whether people were prisoner of war, whether they were civilians, whether they were military, disciplinary detainees. Did you -- did anyone at the prison during June 1993 know the categories or classification of any of these people, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: As for knowledge, Mr. Vidovic and his men from the crime investigations service and the SIS processed every single one of them and only they knew who were the military prisoners, in fact prisoners of war, and we found out only in June when only prisoners of war were left in the prison. Until then we didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you said you found out in June, in June of what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not following you, sir. You're saying that all -- all the other people -- everyone was taken out of the prison except the prisoners of war in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: In June 1993, all those who were brought on the 9th of May were released, and then all military detainees remained until the 30th of June when new people were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's be sure that our terminology -- we are an agreeing on terminology. When you say military detainees - I'm looking at the transcript - when you use that terminology, are you talking about member of the HVO who were being -- who were subject to some sort of a disciplinary action?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I want to make sure I'm following you. So are you saying -- do we understand you to be saying that at the end of June all of those persons were taken out of the Heliodrom prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I thought I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: When the people, in fact women and children left on the 9th of May, only one category of prisoners were left, military detainees and military prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me come at it from a different direction. Let's jump ahead a month and see if we can get any further -- at the end of July, 1993, who was being held at the Heliodrom prison? Were they all prisoners of war, or was there a mixture, or what can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: In the prison there was still physical separation between military prisoners and prisoners of war. They were physically separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: After the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever receive lists from Mr. Vidovic of the list -- the copies of the list that he and his group had made? I know you told us that Mr. Bozic later had other lists prepared, but my question to you now is: Did you ever receive the list that Mr. Vidovic and his group prepared?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: If the list was received, it was received in May. Sorry, in September. Then, in September we got a list of all those who would remain and against whom a criminal report was filed. The others -- in fact other lists were received when those prisoners of war were released, so that we had that it at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be told that he can speak in normal sentences. He doesn't have to cut them into little bits and pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you, sir, was this -- did this happen in September or December of 1993, the releases that you're talking about now?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I think it happened in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, did there -- we talked about the releases that took place after the 9th of May, and we looked at a number of documents about -- in connection with the people being released after the 9th of May. Was there a similar procedure or any procedure for the release of individual prisoners who were brought in around the 30th of June, 1993, and thereafter?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: These prisoners of war were released in a different way than before. On that occasion, the release was handled by the crime investigations service, the SIS, and the signatory was the head of the exchange office, Mr. Berislav Pusic. And most documents on release were issued that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us a bit more of what various approvals or -- yes, let me say that. What approvals were required, to your knowledge, to have a prisoner released from the Heliodrom in July, August 1993? You can just walk us through whatever steps were taken, if you can help us, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: The document that would reach us in the prison was formulated like this, approximately: "There is no reason to hold the prisoner of war such-and-such," and it would be signed by Miroslav Music on behalf of the SIS and Zvonko Vidovic on behalf of the crime investigation service. They would issue approvals enabling Mr. Berko Pusic to release somebody. I believe without these two signatures above, Mr. Berislav Pusic would have been unable to release anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you said a few moments ago that it required the head of the exchange office, and I think you actually did wind up saying it here, sorry, I do see it on page 89. Do you know what the function of the exchange office, what you've described as the exchange office, what the functions or operations of that particular office was?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: The head of that office for exchange, Mr. Berislav Pusic, probably effected exchanges and releases of prisoners of war ex officio, and that speaks enough about the office itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, when you say in that context "ex officio" or at least what's transcribed ex officio, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Berislav Pusic, as head of that office for exchange, took care of the prisoners of war and was aware of each and every prisoner of war who was brought to Heliodrom or was already held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look at Exhibit P 04379.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 4379. Thank you. If you have that now, Mr. Praljak, can you tell us what that document is?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. That's the document that I described a moment ago. In fact, I described a moment ago the way in which a prisoner of war was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This -- at the top of the document it says "Personally to the warden of the military detention --" or "VIZ," leave it at that, "Stanko Bozic."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall how these documents would be transmitted to Mr. Bozic and to your office at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Most of these documents were brought by officials probably of the office for exchange. Mr. Jerko Radic was the one who came most often, and Tomo Sakota. I think he was the one who spent the most time down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is this document we're looking at now, 4379, would you consider that to be representative of the type of document that was used during this time period for the release of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, when you look at the form in the original language, is it fair to say that the document itself looks like a form with certain blanks that would indeed be filled in when the document was used on various occasions?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I couldn't say that, because after all these approvals were issued in the office of Berislav Pusic or Zvonko Vidovic or a third person, Music. I can't really say, because I only received them when they were already filled in and reached us at the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell us anything more about the relationship between - if any - between Mr. Vidovic and Mr. Pusic, if you know? I mean in terms it of the working relationship, any experiences you had in working with the two of them together?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to object to this kind of question, because this witness cannot tell us about the relationship between Mr. Vidovic and Mr. Pusic. He can tell us about his relationship with Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's just simply not true, Your Honour. He may have firsthand knowledge of the relationship between the two of them. He may know, and I have reason to think that he does know. So if he can remember. If he doesn't remember, I'll certainly pass on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But, sir, can you tell us about any relationship you know of between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you answer this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know both Mr. Zvonko Vidovic and Mr. Berko Pusic, and I still know them today. Both Zvonko Vidovic in Mostar who meets with me occasionally. I don't know what I'm supposed to say. What are you interested in?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question was the relationship, if you knew, between Mr. Pusic Vidovic at that time. Were they close friends? Did they associate frequently? Did they have family relations?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may -- if I may assist in the objection before that. It presupposes that they had a relationship. The form of the question has an element of -- of -- that there was a relationship. I think if it was rephrased: Was there a relationship? If so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it, Your Honour. It's late in the day but I'm happy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you know of any relationship between Mr. Vidovic and Mr. Pusic during the time that these events were occurring in 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Zvonko Vidovic and Mr. Berislav Pusic both worked at the military police as investigators in the crime prevention service, and of course in their line of work they were close. And of course anybody, including myself, with Mr. Stanko would be close to somebody who's working with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was there any family relationship between the two of them and their families?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I don't know about family affairs. I wouldn't like to discuss that. That could be misunderstood, and it would lead us astray. I don't think we should go into family matters, at least not before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you about -- after these men were brought in and processed by Mr. Vidovic and his group, the MUP, military police, SIS, can you tell the Judges whether these prisoners were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: I couldn't confirm. All I know is that the processing was done by those 10 or 12 people led by Mr. Vidovic, and it's probable that at the end when they made the triage and identified who the prisoners of war were they had to reinterrogate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were working at the Heliodrom prison during this time period. After these people were taken in by Mr. Vidovic and the others, were SIS -- members of SIS, the military police, others coming on a regular basis to the Heliodrom to interrogate prisoners there? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise but I have to interject. Maybe there is a misunderstanding due to interpretation, but he didn't say of that he was -- that these people were brought to Heliodrom by Mr. Vidovic and the others. He said they were listed and processed by Mr. Vidovic and others, but no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Maybe it was translation, Your Honour; I'm sorry, but I think it was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The people that were brought in and processed by Mr. Vidovic and others, sir, can you tell us whether these men were interrogated at the Heliodrom after that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were all -- MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I am sorry, my learned friend. I believe there is a mistake in the record, but even now the record says "brought in by Vidovic" and "listed by Vidovic." Maybe you could divide your question into two parts to divide those who were brought in on the 30th of June and then listed, because the transcript remains wrong and it's important for later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please make that more precise?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the prisoners that were brought in on the 30th of June and thereafter, were they interrogated?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: By who? What --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: Zvonko Vidovic with his group of 10 to 12 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know whether they were all interrogated at the Heliodrom, or can you tell the Judges whether people were also taken away to other locations and interrogated?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: A smaller number of people, as we can see from the records, were taken away by the SIS for interrogation. Most of them, however, were interrogated at the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what -- how would the arrangements be made -- excuse me. How would the arrangements be made for the purposes of taking prisoners away from the Heliodrom for purposes of interrogation? Who had to sign off on that? What kind of a record was made?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK
utterances.text: There was a paper trail, an order from the commander or the chief, what's his name, in the SIS, Mr. Ivo Lucic or Mr. Zvonko Sesar, ordering the prison that persons such-and-such would be taken over by an officer of the SIS, and that the same officer would conduct an interview with the named person, who would then be returned to the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: While there's a small break, can you tell us do you know where such persons were taken for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only suppose, because they had their own building and their own premises where they did their job. We were not able to know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, looking at the clock, I'm about to turn to a new document, and I'm not sure I will be able to finish it in the next two minutes, so I wonder if we might break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are going to adjourn. I believe that by and large you have used up two hours, so you have four hours to go. In fact, you have used two hours, 29 minutes. That's what the registrar tells me. I thought it was less. So tomorrow you have, on balance, around four hours, and you have to complete your examination-in-chief tomorrow. Witness, we are coming back to this courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m. Not in this courtroom but courtroom number III. And I hope that these many kilos of documents will be moved to the third -- to the second floor. So until tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
